## Three words

Verified, documented, and open, and what each means. Verified means somebody ran it and recorded the result. Documented means it was read in documentation and not tested here. Open means it is genuinely unsettled, and the page should say what would settle it rather than leaving the word to imply doubt about everything nearby.

The distinction the site cannot afford to blur is the first two. Presenting something read as something run is the one failure that would make the guide untrustworthy.

## Inheritance

Page-level and column-level tags, and what an untagged claim means. Stated here once and nowhere else, because a rule restated on every page is itself the clutter.

Confidence is per-claim rather than per-page, so a single page can hold all three kinds. The rule for an untagged claim has to be stated explicitly here, because most claims on the site are untagged and the reader will infer some rule whether or not one is given.

## The machine

One workspace, and the session size, node count, runtime version and access mode for each recorded run.

The node count matters more than the rest, because a single-node cluster cannot demonstrate distribution and will pass almost any test written to check it. Any number about parallel work is only readable alongside the node count of the machine that produced it.

## Why no number here is a benchmark

Single runs. Warehouse submit latency varies by up to 6.5x, and results cache. Two sources of variation that large mean a single timing cannot support a comparison, and the site does not ask it to: the numbers are there to show an order of magnitude and to be honest about where they came from.

## What is open, in one place

With the reason each one is open, and what would settle it. Two are known now: whether `spark_apply()` runs under Standard access mode, which needs a cluster that has to be created rather than started, and how distributed R work scales, where two workers has been observed and says nothing about twenty.
